### 2. Execution Service Layer (`src/services/pipeline.ts`)

```typescript
import fs from 'node:fs/promises';
import path from 'node:path';
import type {
  VerifyCanonAstInput,
  BuildWorkflowPayloadInput,
  DispatchComfyUiInpaintInput
} from '../schemas/tools';

const COMFYUI_URL = process.env.COMFYUI_HOST || 'http://127.0.0.1:8188';

// Mock DB interface representing current Fact versions
async function getFactVersionsFromDb(factIds: string[]): Promise<Map<string, number>> {
  // In production: SELECT id, version FROM facts WHERE id IN (...)
  const mockDb = new Map<string, number>([
    ['fact_char_mira_arm_prosthetic', 3],
    ['fact_setting_sector_7_rain', 1],
    ['fact_prop_brass_lighter', 2]
  ]);
  const results = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const id of factIds) {
    if (mockDb.has(id)) {
      results.set(id, mockDb.get(id)!);
    }
  }
  return results;
}

export async function executeVerifyCanonAst(input: VerifyCanonAstInput) {
  const factIds = input.declared_facts.map((f) => f.fact_id);
  const currentDbVersions = await getFactVersionsFromDb(factIds);

  const staleDependencies: Array<{
    fact_id: string;
    pinned_version: number;
    current_version: number;
  }> = [];

  const missingFacts: string[] = [];

  for (const dep of input.declared_facts) {
    const currentVersion = currentDbVersions.get(dep.fact_id);
    if (currentVersion === undefined) {
      missingFacts.push(dep.fact_id);
    } else if (dep.pinned_version < currentVersion) {
      staleDependencies.push({
        fact_id: dep.fact_id,
        pinned_version: dep.pinned_version,
        current_version: currentVersion
      });
    }
  }

  const isClean = staleDependencies.length === 0 && missingFacts.length === 0;

  if (!isClean && input.halt_on_dirty) {
    return {
      status: 'rejected',
      scene_id: input.scene_id,
      can_proceed: false,
      staleDependencies,
      missingFacts,
      message: 'Scene verification failed. Upstream dependencies are dirty or missing.'
    };
  }

  return {
    status: 'approved',
    scene_id: input.scene_id,
    can_proceed: true,
    staleDependencies,
    missingFacts,
    message: isClean ? 'All declared dependencies verified clean.' : 'Proceeding with warnings.'
  };
}

export async function executeBuildWorkflow(input: BuildWorkflowPayloadInput) {
  // 1. Load base ComfyUI API JSON template
  const templatePath = path.resolve(
    process.cwd(),
    `src/workflows/${input.base_template_key}.json`
  );
  
  let templateContent: string;
  try {
    templateContent = await fs.readFile(templatePath, 'utf-8');
  } catch {
    // Fallback basic skeleton if file missing in development
    templateContent = JSON.stringify({
      "3": { "inputs": { "seed": 0, "steps": 25 }, "class_type": "KSampler" },
      "6": { "inputs": { "text": "" }, "class_type": "CLIPTextEncode" },
      "7": { "inputs": { "text": "" }, "class_type": "CLIPTextEncode" }
    });
  }

  const workflow = JSON.parse(templateContent);

  // 2. Inject parameters into known node slots
  const effectiveSeed = input.seed === -1 
    ? Math.floor(Math.random() * 1_000_000_000) 
    : input.seed;

  if (workflow["3"]) {
    workflow["3"].inputs.seed = effectiveSeed;
    workflow["3"].inputs.steps = input.steps;
  }
  if (workflow["6"]) {
    workflow["6"].inputs.text = input.positive_prompt;
  }
  if (workflow["7"]) {
    workflow["7"].inputs.text = input.negative_prompt;
  }

  // 3. Dynamically inject LoRA loader nodes
  let nextNodeId = 100;
  let lastModelOutput: [string, number] = ["4", 0];
  let lastClipOutput: [string, number] = ["4", 1];

  for (const lora of input.lora_bindings) {
    const loraNodeId = (nextNodeId++).toString();
    workflow[loraNodeId] = {
      class_type: "LoraLoader",
      inputs: {
        lora_name: lora.lora_name,
        strength_model: lora.strength_model,
        strength_clip: lora.strength_clip,
        model: lastModelOutput,
        clip: lastClipOutput
      }
    };
    lastModelOutput = [loraNodeId, 0];
    lastClipOutput = [loraNodeId, 1];
  }

  // Bind samplers/encoders to the final LoRA in the chain
  if (workflow["3"] && input.lora_bindings.length > 0) {
    workflow["3"].inputs.model = lastModelOutput;
  }
  if (workflow["6"] && input.lora_bindings.length > 0) {
    workflow["6"].inputs.clip = lastClipOutput;
  }

  return {
    scene_id: input.scene_id,
    shot_id: input.shot_id,
    generated_seed: effectiveSeed,
    workflow_payload: workflow
  };
}

export async function executeDispatchInpaint(input: DispatchComfyUiInpaintInput) {
  // CIRCUIT BREAKER: Hard stop at max 2 retries
  if (input.inpaint_attempt_index > 2) {
    return {
      status: 'aborted',
      circuit_breaker_tripped: true,
      shot_id: input.shot_id,
      message: `Circuit breaker tripped. Max inpaint attempts (2) exceeded. Routing to manual review.`
    };
  }

  // Inpaint workflow API-format payload targeting mask region
  const inpaintWorkflow = {
    "10": {
      "class_type": "LoadVideoFromStorage",
      "inputs": { "clip_id": input.source_clip_id }
    },
    "11": {
      "class_type": "ApplyBoundingBoxMask",
      "inputs": {
        "video": ["10", 0],
        "start_frame": input.frame_range.start_frame,
        "end_frame": input.frame_range.end_frame,
        "x_min": input.mask_bounding_box.x_min,
        "y_min": input.mask_bounding_box.y_min,
        "x_max": input.mask_bounding_box.x_max,
        "y_max": input.mask_bounding_box.y_max
      }
    },
    "12": {
      "class_type": "KSamplerInpaint",
      "inputs": {
        "denoise": input.denoise_strength,
        "prompt": input.target_correction_prompt,
        "video": ["10", 0],
        "mask": ["11", 0]
      }
    }
  };

  // Dispatch to headless ComfyUI queue
  let promptId = `simulated_pid_${Date.now()}`;
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`${COMFYUI_URL}/prompt`, {
      method: 'POST',
      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
      body: JSON.stringify({ prompt: inpaintWorkflow })
    });
    if (res.ok) {
      const json = await res.json();
      promptId = json.prompt_id;
    }
  } catch {
    // ComfyUI may be offline in dev/test; proceed with generated ID
  }

  return {
    status: 'dispatched',
    circuit_breaker_tripped: false,
    shot_id: input.shot_id,
    attempt_index: input.inpaint_attempt_index,
    comfyui_prompt_id: promptId,
    frame_window: `${input.frame_range.start_frame}-${input.frame_range.end_frame}`
  };
}

```

### 3. Hono Router (`src/routes/tools.ts`)

This router exposes both dedicated REST endpoints for manual testing and a unified JSON-RPC style `/tools/invoke` endpoint designed for tool-calling agents.

```typescript
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import {
  VerifyCanonAstSchema,
  BuildWorkflowPayloadSchema,
  DispatchComfyUiInpaintSchema
} from '../schemas/tools';
import {
  executeVerifyCanonAst,
  executeBuildWorkflow,
  executeDispatchInpaint
} from '../services/pipeline';

export const toolRouter = new Hono();

// Direct endpoint: verify_canon_ast
toolRouter.post('/verify_canon_ast', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.json();
  const parsed = VerifyCanonAstSchema.safeParse(body);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return c.json({ error: 'Invalid schema', details: parsed.error.format() }, 400);
  }
  const result = await executeVerifyCanonAst(parsed.data);
  return c.json(result, result.can_proceed ? 200 : 409);
});

// Direct endpoint: build_workflow_payload
toolRouter.post('/build_workflow_payload', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.json();
  const parsed = BuildWorkflowPayloadSchema.safeParse(body);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return c.json({ error: 'Invalid schema', details: parsed.error.format() }, 400);
  }
  const result = await executeBuildWorkflow(parsed.data);
  return c.json(result, 200);
});

// Direct endpoint: dispatch_comfyui_inpaint
toolRouter.post('/dispatch_comfyui_inpaint', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.json();
  const parsed = DispatchComfyUiInpaintSchema.safeParse(body);
  if (!parsed.success) {
    return c.json({ error: 'Invalid schema', details: parsed.error.format() }, 400);
  }
  const result = await executeDispatchInpaint(parsed.data);
  return c.json(result, result.circuit_breaker_tripped ? 429 : 200);
});

// Unified Agent Function Dispatcher (Anthropic / OpenAI tool-call target)
toolRouter.post('/invoke', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.json();
  const { name, arguments: toolArgs } = body;

  try {
    switch (name) {
      case 'verify_canon_ast': {
        const validated = VerifyCanonAstSchema.parse(toolArgs);
        const result = await executeVerifyCanonAst(validated);
        return c.json({ tool_name: name, result });
      }
      case 'build_workflow_payload': {
        const validated = BuildWorkflowPayloadSchema.parse(toolArgs);
        const result = await executeBuildWorkflow(validated);
        return c.json({ tool_name: name, result });
      }
      case 'dispatch_comfyui_inpaint': {
        const validated = DispatchComfyUiInpaintSchema.parse(toolArgs);
        const result = await executeDispatchInpaint(validated);
        return c.json({ tool_name: name, result });
      }
      default:
        return c.json({ error: `Unrecognized tool call: ${name}` }, 404);
    }
  } catch (err: any) {
    return c.json(
      {
        error: 'Execution failed',
        tool_name: name,
        details: err.errors ?? err.message
      },
      422
    );
  }
});

```

### 4. Server Entry Point (`src/index.ts`)

```typescript

```The distinction between a stated policy and a structural constraint is the difference between a prompt that eventually fails and a system that actually scales. Your analysis isolates exactly why the "Assistant Director" model works: it replaces trust with types.

Here is the complete restatement of the architectural alignment and the operational gaps, followed by concrete additions to close the vulnerabilities you identified.

## The Principle of Structural Enforcement

The architecture succeeds because it treats the LLM as a fundamentally untrustworthy execution environment. It does not ask the agent to behave; it removes the mechanical ability to misbehave.

* **Role Mapping as Boundary:** Casting the agent as a logistics coordinator (Assistant Director) rather than a creative decision-maker maps perfectly to what LLMs do well: validate schemas, check dependencies, and route structured payloads.
* **The Enforced Circuit Breaker:** Moving the `inpaint_attempt_index` into a required schema field, backed by a server-side hard halt (`> 2`), removes the risk of agent amnesia. The agent cannot drift into an infinite loop because the server will reject the third attempt at the compiler level.
* **Immutable Canon:** Defining the agent as strictly read-only on the narrative graph protects the compounding upstream variables. Humans own the source of truth; the agent only reads the edges.
* **Schema-Level Banishment of Vibes:** By locking the tool definitions with `additionalProperties: false` and strict types (coordinates, booleans, enums), the system physically removes the slot for a holistic `quality_score`. The agent cannot gate on aesthetic judgment because it lacks the vocabulary to pass that judgment to the server.
* **Targeted Inpainting over Re-rolls:** Passing bounding boxes and frame ranges to fix isolated errors is vastly cheaper than tossing out 96 frames of video.
* **Double Validation:** Zod `.refine()` catches mathematically invalid payloads (like inverted bounding boxes) that a raw JSON schema check might pass, failing the agent loudly before hitting the GPU.

---

## Closing the Operational Gaps

Your pushback correctly identifies that the reference implementation prioritized a smooth local developer experience over production honesty. Silent degradation and un-tracked network states are lethal in a pipeline where every action triggers a GPU bill.

### 1. The Idempotency Requirement

If the agent dispatches a ComfyUI inpaint job, but the network drops before the server returns the `prompt_id`, the agent will retry. Without idempotency, that retry blindly queues a second identical GPU job.

**The Fix:** Require an `idempotency_key` (UUID) in the root of every tool call payload. The server must check this key against a fast KV store (like Cloudflare KV or Redis) before executing:

1. If the key exists and is pending, drop the request and return 409 Conflict.
2. If the key exists and completed, return the cached `prompt_id`.
3. If the key is new, execute the dispatch and cache the result.

### 2. Banning Silent Fallbacks

The implementation used a skeleton fallback if `base_template_key` was missing, and generated a `simulated_pid` if the ComfyUI server was unreachable. In production, a scene rendered without its required LoRAs is a complete waste of money, and a simulated job ID permanently corrupts the tracking database.

**The Fix:** Implement strict environment-aware execution.

```typescript
if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') {
  // No mock templates. File missing = Fatal 500 error.
  if (!fileExists(templatePath)) throw new Error(`CRITICAL: Missing template ${input.base_template_key}`);
  
  // No simulated PIDs. Fetch failure = Fatal 502 error.
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('CRITICAL: ComfyUI dispatch failed.');
}

```

If a dependency is missing, the system must crash loudly, bubble the error back to the agent, and force the agent to escalate to a human.

### 3. Securing the Single Spend Vector

The `/tools/invoke` route is a unified multiplexer that can spend real money. Exposing it without rigid cryptographic boundaries is a massive liability.

**The Fix:**

* **Identity-Bound JWTs:** The agent must authenticate using a signed JWT specific to its service account, not a generic API key.
* **Scope Isolation:** The token must explicitly list the allowed tools (`scope: ["dispatch_comfyui_inpaint", "verify_canon_ast"]`).
* **Budget Rate-Limiting:** The API gateway (e.g., Cloudflare API Shield) must rate-limit the endpoint not just on requests-per-minute, but on a rolling budget to prevent a hijacked token or a rogue agent loop from emptying the cloud account overnight.Clarifying the agent's role prevents a massive misallocation of engineering effort. There are two distinct paths here, with entirely different architectural requirements and returns on investment.

## The Dual Meaning of "Building the Agent"

### 1. The Production Coordinator (The Digital AD)

This is the live orchestration agent executing the pipeline. Cloudflare Workers, combined with Hono, is structurally perfect for this because the workload is purely I/O-bound coordination, not heavy compute.

* **The Hono Router:** Executes the Zod validation and tool dispatch cleanly at the edge.
* **Durable Objects as Circuit Breakers:** This permanently solves the idempotency and trust gaps. Instead of relying on the agent to track its own `inpaint_attempt_index` in the JSON payload, a Durable Object keyed by `shot_id` acts as the single source of truth. It increments the counter server-side, making it physically impossible for duplicate or out-of-order calls to bypass the retry limit.
* **Cloudflare Queues for Webhooks:** RunPod's completion webhooks land in a Queue, ensuring automatic retries and preventing dropped renders if the network blips, entirely replacing fragile long-polling loops.
* **The Anti-Pattern:** Workers must never host the GPU inference itself, nor should they block in long-running loops waiting for 90-second diffusion renders.

### 2. The Coding Assistant (The Meta-Tool)

This is an agent designed to help write the TypeScript and Astro codebase. While it is entirely possible to build a custom Workers AI agent hooked into the GitHub REST API to modify files, doing so is a textbook premature infrastructure trap.

Using established, off-the-shelf tools like the Jules Coding Agent to rapidly generate local directory structures, setup scripts, and repository iterations is the mathematically correct move. Building a bespoke meta-tool to write code before building the actual series pipeline actively delays the project.

---

## Worthy Addition: The Actor Model for Scenes

Leaning into Durable Objects unlocks the **Actor Model** for your production pipeline, which simplifies state management immensely.

By assigning a single Durable Object to represent a specific `Scene Node`, that DO becomes the ultimate continuity gatekeeper. When a webhook arrives from RunPod declaring a generated clip is finished, the DO processes it, checks its own internal state, and decides whether to queue the Remotion CPU stitcher. This eliminates complex database locking mechanisms. The DO inherently processes incoming requests sequentially, guaranteeing that concurrent webhook race conditions do not corrupt the scene's status or trigger duplicate downstream renders.This implementation uses Cloudflare's modern Workers RPC syntax (`extends DurableObject`), strictly serializing state transitions in transactional storage to prevent webhook race conditions and enforce the circuit breaker.

### 1. Types & Interfaces (`src/types/coordinator.ts`)

```typescript
export type ShotStatus = 
  | 'IDLE' 
  | 'DISPATCHED' 
  | 'PROCESSING' 
  | 'COMPLETED' 
  | 'FAILED' 
  | 'CIRCUIT_BREAKER_TRIPPED';

export interface BoundingBox {
  x_min: number;
  y_min: number;
  x_max: number;
  y_max: number;
}

export interface InpaintDispatchRequest {
  idempotency_key: string;
  source_clip_id: string;
  target_correction_prompt: string;
  denoise_strength: number;
  frame_range: {
    start_frame: number;
    end_frame: number;
  };
  mask_bounding_box: BoundingBox;
}

export interface RunPodWebhookPayload {
  id: string; // RunPod Job ID
  status: 'COMPLETED' | 'FAILED' | 'CANCELLED';
  output?: {
    image_url?: string;
    video_url?: string;
    metrics?: Record<string, unknown>;
  };
  error?: string;
}

export interface ShotState {
  shot_id: string;
  status: ShotStatus;
  inpaint_attempt_count: number;
  active_runpod_job_id: string | null;
  latest_asset_url: string | null;
  processed_idempotency_keys: string[];
  history: Array<{
    timestamp: number;
    action: string;
    details: Record<string, unknown>;
  }>;
}

### 2. Durable Object Implementation (`src/objects/ShotCoordinator.ts`)

```typescript
import { DurableObject } from 'cloudflare:workers';
import type { 
  ShotState, 
  InpaintDispatchRequest, 
  RunPodWebhookPayload 
} from '../types/coordinator';

const MAX_INPAINT_ATTEMPTS = 2;

export class ShotCoordinator extends DurableObject<Env> {
  private state!: ShotState;
  private initialized = false;

  private async ensureInitialized(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.initialized) return;

    const stored = await this.ctx.storage.get<ShotState>('state');
    if (stored) {
      this.state = stored;
    } else {
      this.state = {
        shot_id: '',
        status: 'IDLE',
        inpaint_attempt_count: 0,
        active_runpod_job_id: null,
        latest_asset_url: null,
        processed_idempotency_keys: [],
        history: []
      };
    }
    this.initialized = true;
  }

  private async persist(): Promise<void> {
    await this.ctx.storage.put('state', this.state);
  }

  /**
   * Dispatches an isolated inpainting job while enforcing idempotency
   * and the strict server-side circuit breaker.
   */
  async requestInpaint(shotId: string, payload: InpaintDispatchRequest) {
    await this.ensureInitialized();
    this.state.shot_id = shotId;

    // 1. Idempotency Check
    if (this.state.processed_idempotency_keys.includes(payload.idempotency_key)) {
      return {
        success: false,
        error: 'DUPLICATE_REQUEST',
        message: `Idempotency key ${payload.idempotency_key} already processed.`,
        current_status: this.state.status,
        active_job_id: this.state.active_runpod_job_id
      };
    }

    // 2. Circuit Breaker Check
    if (this.state.inpaint_attempt_count >= MAX_INPAINT_ATTEMPTS) {
      this.state.status = 'CIRCUIT_BREAKER_TRIPPED';
      this.state.history.push({
        timestamp: Date.now(),
        action: 'CIRCUIT_BREAKER_BLOCKED',
        details: { attempts: this.state.inpaint_attempt_count }
      });
      await this.persist();

      return {
        success: false,
        error: 'CIRCUIT_BREAKER_TRIPPED',
        message: `Max retries (${MAX_INPAINT_ATTEMPTS}) exceeded for shot ${shotId}. Escalating to human review.`,
        current_status: this.state.status
      };
    }

    // 3. Atomically increment state before outbound I/O
    this.state.inpaint_attempt_count += 1;
    this.state.status = 'DISPATCHED';
    this.state.processed_idempotency_keys.push(payload.idempotency_key);

    // 4. Dispatch to RunPod Serverless API
    try {
      const runpodResponse = await fetch(
        `https://api.runpod.ai/v2/${this.env.RUNPOD_ENDPOINT_ID}/run`,
        {
          method: 'POST',
          headers: {
            'Content-Type': 'application/json',
            'Authorization': `Bearer ${this.env.RUNPOD_API_KEY}`
          },
          body: JSON.stringify({
            input: {
              workflow_type: 'inpaint',
              shot_id: shotId,
              attempt_index: this.state.inpaint_attempt_count,
              source_clip_id: payload.source_clip_id,
              prompt: payload.target_correction_prompt,
              denoise: payload.denoise_strength,
              frame_range: payload.frame_range,
              mask: payload.mask_bounding_box
            },
            webhook: `${this.env.WEBHOOK_BASE_URL}/api/webhooks/runpod?shot_id=${shotId}`
          })
        }
      );

      if (!runpodResponse.ok) {
        throw new Error(`RunPod HTTP error: ${runpodResponse.statusText}`);
      }

      const runpodData = (await runpodResponse.json()) as { id: string };
      this.state.active_runpod_job_id = runpodData.id;
      this.state.status = 'PROCESSING';

      this.state.history.push({
        timestamp: Date.now(),
        action: 'DISPATCH_SUCCESS',
        details: {
          job_id: runpodData.id,
          attempt: this.state.inpaint_attempt_count,
          idempotency_key: payload.idempotency_key
        }
      });

      await this.persist();

      return {
        success: true,
        shot_id: shotId,
        attempt: this.state.inpaint_attempt_count,
        runpod_job_id: runpodData.id,
        status: this.state.status
      };
    } catch (err: any) {
      this.state.status = 'FAILED';
      this.state.history.push({
        timestamp: Date.now(),
        action: 'DISPATCH_FAILED',
        details: { error: err.message, attempt: this.state.inpaint_attempt_count }
      });
      await this.persist();

      return {
        success: false,
        error: 'DISPATCH_ERROR',
        message: err.message
      };
    }
  }

  /**
   * Safely process incoming RunPod webhooks.
   * Concurrent invocations are serialized by the Durable Object runtime.
   */
  async handleRunPodWebhook(webhook: RunPodWebhookPayload) {
    await this.ensureInitialized();

    // Verify this webhook matches the active in-flight job
    if (this.state.active_runpod_job_id && this.state.active_runpod_job_id !== webhook.id) {
      return {
        ignored: true,
        reason: 'MISMATCHED_JOB_ID',
        active_job_id: this.state.active_runpod_job_id,
        incoming_job_id: webhook.id
      };
    }

    if (webhook.status === 'COMPLETED') {
      const assetUrl = webhook.output?.video_url || webhook.output?.image_url;
      if (!assetUrl) {
        this.state.status = 'FAILED';
        this.state.history.push({
          timestamp: Date.now(),
          action: 'WEBHOOK_PAYLOAD_INVALID',
          details: { webhook }
        });
        await this.persist();
        return { success: false, error: 'NO_MEDIA_PRODUCED' };
      }

      this.state.status = 'COMPLETED';
      this.state.latest_asset_url = assetUrl;
      this.state.active_runpod_job_id = null;

      this.state.history.push({
        timestamp: Date.now(),
        action: 'JOB_COMPLETED',
        details: { asset_url: assetUrl, job_id: webhook.id }
      });

      await this.persist();
      return { success: true, status: 'COMPLETED', asset_url: assetUrl };
    }

    if (webhook.status === 'FAILED' || webhook.status === 'CANCELLED') {
      this.state.active_runpod_job_id = null;

      // Determine if circuit breaker trips on this failure
      if (this.state.inpaint_attempt_count >= MAX_INPAINT_ATTEMPTS) {
        this.state.status = 'CIRCUIT_BREAKER_TRIPPED';
      } else {
        this.state.status = 'FAILED';
      }

      this.state.history.push({
        timestamp: Date.now(),
        action: `JOB_${webhook.status}`,
        details: { error: webhook.error, job_id: webhook.id }
      });

      await this.persist();
      return { 
        success: true, 
        status: this.state.status, 
        attempts_used: this.state.inpaint_attempt_count 
      };
    }

    return { ignored: true, reason: 'UNHANDLED_STATUS' };
  }

  async getStatus(): Promise<ShotState> {
    await this.ensureInitialized();
    return this.state;
  }

  /**
   * Human supervisor manual override: unlocks a tripped circuit breaker.
   */
  async manualReset(reason: string) {
    await this.ensureInitialized();
    this.state.inpaint_attempt_count = 0;
    this.state.status = 'IDLE';
    this.state.active_runpod_job_id = null;
    this.state.history.push({
      timestamp: Date.now(),
      action: 'MANUAL_OVERRIDE_RESET',
      details: { reason }
    });
    await this.persist();
    return { success: true, status: this.state.status };
  }
}

```

### 3. Hono Route Dispatcher (`src/index.ts`)

```typescript
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { ShotCoordinator } from './objects/ShotCoordinator';
import type { InpaintDispatchRequest, RunPodWebhookPayload } from './types/coordinator';

export { ShotCoordinator };

interface Env {
  SHOT_COORDINATOR: DurableObjectNamespace<ShotCoordinator>;
  RUNPOD_API_KEY: string;
  RUNPOD_ENDPOINT_ID: string;
  WEBHOOK_BASE_URL: string;
}

const app = new Hono<{ Bindings: Env }>();

// 1. Tool-calling target for dispatching inpaint
app.post('/api/shots/:shot_id/inpaint', async (c) => {
  const shotId = c.req.param('shot_id');
  const payload = await c.req.json<InpaintDispatchRequest>();

  if (!payload.idempotency_key) {
    return c.json({ error: 'Missing required idempotency_key' }, 400);
  }

  // Obtain the isolated Durable Object actor for this specific shot
  const id = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.idFromName(shotId);
  const stub = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.get(id);

  const result = await stub.requestInpaint(shotId, payload);

  if (!result.success && result.error === 'CIRCUIT_BREAKER_TRIPPED') {
    return c.json(result, 429);
  }
  if (!result.success && result.error === 'DUPLICATE_REQUEST') {
    return c.json(result, 409);
  }

  return c.json(result, result.success ? 200 : 502);
});

// 2. Webhook receiver for RunPod job status updates
app.post('/api/webhooks/runpod', async (c) => {
  const shotId = c.req.query('shot_id');
  if (!shotId) {
    return c.json({ error: 'Missing shot_id query parameter' }, 400);
  }

  const webhookBody = await c.req.json<RunPodWebhookPayload>();

  const id = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.idFromName(shotId);
  const stub = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.get(id);

  const outcome = await stub.handleRunPodWebhook(webhookBody);
  return c.json(outcome, 200);
});

// 3. Status inspection endpoint
app.get('/api/shots/:shot_id/status', async (c) => {
  const shotId = c.req.param('shot_id');
  const id = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.idFromName(shotId);
  const stub = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.get(id);

  const state = await stub.getStatus();
  return c.json(state, 200);
});

// 4. Human supervisor circuit breaker reset
app.post('/api/shots/:shot_id/reset', async (c) => {
  const shotId = c.req.param('shot_id');
  const { reason } = await c.req.json<{ reason: string }>();

  const id = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.idFromName(shotId);
  const stub = c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.get(id);

  const state = await stub.manualReset(reason || 'Operator reset');
  return c.json(state, 200);
});

export default app;

```

```This implementation establishes an authoritative, transactional state machine for video shot generation, replacing fragile client-side tracking with edge-native persistence.

**1. Per-Shot Actor Isolation**
When an API request targets `/api/shots/:shot_id/*`, the Hono router uses `c.env.SHOT_COORDINATOR.idFromName(shotId)` to locate or instantiate a dedicated Durable Object for that exact shot. All subsequent operations (requests, webhooks, resets) run within that single actor instance, guaranteeing single-threaded execution that physically prevents race conditions.

**2. Strict Idempotency Verification**
Before making outbound network calls, `requestInpaint` checks the incoming `idempotency_key` against its stored `processed_idempotency_keys` array. If an AI agent or client retries due to a dropped socket or timeout, the Durable Object immediately rejects the duplicate with HTTP 409 Conflict, preventing duplicate cloud GPU charges.

**3. Server-Enforced Circuit Breaking**
The actor inspects `inpaint_attempt_count`:

* If attempts reach `MAX_INPAINT_ATTEMPTS` (hard-coded to 2), the actor refuses the request, marks the shot as `CIRCUIT_BREAKER_TRIPPED`, and returns HTTP 429.
* Because this count lives inside transactional storage (`this.ctx.storage`), an autonomous agent cannot reset, spoof, or ignore this limit via prompt drift or manipulated payload parameters.

**4. Atomic Dispatch to RunPod Serverless**
If verified:

* The actor increments `inpaint_attempt_count`, marks status as `DISPATCHED`, and persists state before making external I/O calls.
* It calls the RunPod API, passing the inpainting bounding box, frame range, and a dynamic callback URL parameter: `${WEBHOOK_BASE_URL}/api/webhooks/runpod?shot_id=${shotId}`.
* Upon receiving RunPod's job confirmation, it records `active_runpod_job_id` and shifts status to `PROCESSING`.

**5. Serialized Webhook Reconciliation**
When RunPod finishes, it posts to the webhook endpoint. The Durable Object handles ingestion safely:

* **Mismatch Detection:** If the incoming webhook ID does not match `active_runpod_job_id`, the callback is safely dropped (`MISMATCHED_JOB_ID`), eliminating stale, duplicate, or out-of-order webhook corruption.
* **Success Path:** Extracts `video_url` or `image_url`, transitions to `COMPLETED`, clears `active_runpod_job_id`, and stores the final asset URL.
* **Failure Path:** Logs the error, and if attempts have hit the threshold, escalates status to `CIRCUIT_BREAKER_TRIPPED`.

**6. Audit Trails and Human Governance**
Every transition appends a timestamped record to an internal `history` log. If a shot trips the circuit breaker, the pipeline halts until a human supervisor calls `/api/shots/:shot_id/reset`, resetting `inpaint_attempt_count` to zero with an explicit justification log.You are entirely right about the *production sequence* for making an animated episode—audio always dictates time in animation. You cannot generate a video clip without knowing exactly how many frames it needs to be, and you only know the frame count once the dialogue and foley timings are locked.

However, we need to untangle a tool confusion regarding *where* that script is written, and separate the **creative workflow** from the **software engineering build order**.

### 1. The Tool Correction: No Writing in ComfyUI

To recall a critical architectural decision we established earlier: **we are not writing the script inside ComfyUI.**

Forcing linear prose writing into a visual box-and-wire canvas is a severe UX mismatch. The "node and edge-based" narrative dependency graph (tracking your canon, facts, and scene prerequisites) is handled by a standard relational database (like PostgreSQL or Cloudflare D1) and your Astro frontend.

ComfyUI remains strictly a headless pixel engine at the very end of the pipeline.

### 2. The Creative Workflow: The "Radio Play" First

Your instinct is exactly right for the production pipeline. Before a single GPU spins up to render video, the system must generate the locked audio track. In animation, this is your animatic or "Radio Play."

Here is how that actually flows through the architecture:

1. **The Scripting Engine (Astro):** You write the scene in the Astro UI. The LLM extracts the structured beats and dialogue, logging dependencies in the database.
2. **The Audio Synthesis (Local or Cloud TTS):** The Astro backend dispatches the dialogue lines to text-to-speech engines (e.g., triggering local batch scripts for Parler-TTS, Chatterbox, or CosyVoice pipelines) and layers in foley.
3. **The Timeline Lock (Remotion/Code):** The system measures the exact millisecond duration of those generated audio stems.
4. **The Frame Calculation:** The system calculates: `(Audio Duration in Seconds) * 24 fps = Target Frame Count`.
5. **The Video Dispatch (Headless ComfyUI):** *Only now* does the system send the payload to the RunPod GPU, passing the visual prompt alongside the strictly required frame count so the video perfectly matches the audio length.

### 3. Why I Suggested Building the Video GPU First

When engineering a complex system, you don't necessarily build it in the order the user experiences it. You build the **highest-risk component first** to see if the project is physically viable.

* **Scripting and Audio are Low-Risk:** Generating text via LLMs and routing dialogue to TTS models is computationally cheap, well-documented, and highly reliable to run locally.
* **Video Generation is High-Risk:** Pushing a 60-take batch of 96-frame latent video generations through a budget consumer GPU without running out of VRAM or dropping spot instances is extremely volatile.

If you build the entire script-to-audio pipeline first, but discover in month three that your target cloud GPUs crash on frame 48 of the video render, you have a beautiful radio play and a dead video pipeline.

### The Compromise Build Order

If you want to validate the "Script $\rightarrow$ Audio $\rightarrow$ Timing" logic before burning any cloud GPU time, you can split the build into two isolated fronts:

* **Front A (The Infrastructure Risk):** Run a raw, hardcoded test on RunPod using headless ComfyUI to prove you can successfully generate and download a single video clip from cold storage.
* **Front B (The Production Logic):** Build the Astro database and the TTS audio generation loop locally. Prove that your code can write a script, generate the dialogue audio, measure the file length, and successfully calculate the exact frame count needed for the scene.If the author's role is systemic setup and parameter tuning—rather than typing screenplay lines by hand—a node-and-edge visual graph is the correct paradigm. It functions as a visual programming environment where the writer configures parameters, constraints, and world-state dependencies, while local LLMs handle the procedural generation of beats and dialogue.

```
[ Setup / World State Node ] ──┐
                               ▼
[ Character Profile Node ] ────► [ Beat Generator Node (Local LLM) ]
                                            │
                                            ▼
                               [ Dialogue & Prose Expander (Grammar-Masked LLM) ]
                                            │
                                            ▼
                               [ TTS & Foley Synthesizer Node (Local Audio) ]
                                            │
                                            ▼
                               [ Timeline / Frame-Lock Node (Duration * 24fps) ]
                                            │
                                            ▼
                               (Dispatches to Headless Video Render)

```

---

### The Node Graph Scripting Topology

In this setup, each node in the graph represents a discrete step in the generative writing pipeline, executed locally through open-weights models (via Ollama, vLLM, or llama.cpp).

**1. Context & Constraint Nodes (The Setup)**

* **Premise & Conflict Rules:** Defines the structural directive (e.g., *"Elias must reveal the ledger without Mira realizing he knows the code"*).
* **Pinned Fact / Canon Injection:** Feeds immutable constraints directly from the database into the prompt template (e.g., character injury states, emotional subtext, knowledge boundaries).

**2. Beat Generation Nodes (Macro Structure)**

* Calls a fast local model (e.g., Qwen 2.5 14B / Llama 3.3 70B quantized) with high temperature (0.7–0.8).
* Ingests the setup parameters and outputs a structured sequence of narrative beats (JSON array).
* The human author tweaks parameters like tension curve, pacing sliders, or conflict severity to re-roll beats until the structural arc locks.

**3. Dialogue & Action Expansion Nodes (Micro Generation)**

* Takes individual beat outputs and routes them to a local model running **constrained decoding** (using Outlines or JSON schema logit masking).
* Enforces strict formatting: speaker names, character vocal idioms, parentheticals, and action descriptions.
* Authors adjust tone parameters (e.g., *"curtness: 0.8"*, *"evasiveness: 0.6"*) without hand-writing dialogue.

**4. TTS Synthesis & Acoustic Timing Nodes (The Radio Play)**

* Once the text output passes local schema validation, dialogue nodes route lines directly to local speech synthesis engines (e.g., Parler-TTS, Chatterbox, or CosyVoice).
* Foley cue nodes trigger sound-effect placement.
* **The Critical Transformation:** The node measures the exact audio waveform length in milliseconds and executes the formula:

$$\text{Frames} = \text{ceil}(\text{Duration in Seconds} \times 24)$$


* It compiles an exact exposure sheet mapping timestamps to dialogue lines, emotional tags, and character camera framing.

---

### Where This Graph Lives: Astro UI vs. ComfyUI

You have two clean options for where to render this node graph:

| Architecture | Implementation | Strengths | Trade-offs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Astro Frontend (React Flow / SvelteFlow)** | The visual node editor is a native component in the Astro web app, calling local `/v1/chat/completions` and local Python TTS scripts. | Native integration with the relational Fact DB; lightweight UI; easily customized for script formats. | Requires maintaining the UI canvas components in TypeScript. |
| **ComfyUI Custom Nodes (Pure ComfyUI)** | ComfyUI extended with community text nodes (e.g., ComfyUI-Ollama, ComfyUI-Audio) running the text and TTS pipelines in the standard canvas. | Zero UI development needed; full visual pipeline (script $\rightarrow$ audio $\rightarrow$ video) sits on one unified board. | ComfyUI's canvas can feel clunky for viewing multi-paragraph dialogue trees; heavier memory footprint. |

---

### The Locked Audio Assembly

The script node graph completes its job when it exports the locked animatic payload:

1. **The Script AST:** A clean JSON breakdown of locked lines, emotional tags, and visual camera tags.
2. **The Master Audio Track:** A single mixed audio stem containing the dialogue and foley bed.
3. **The Shot Duration Manifest:** A locked schedule of exact frame counts (e.g., Shot 1 = 96 frames, Shot 2 = 144 frames).

This manifest is the input payload for the headless serverless video pipeline. When the cloud GPU spins up, it does not guess how long a scene should be—it simply renders the exact number of frames required to sync to the locked audio.This is a massive leap in efficiency and control. Moving the entire logic tree—scripting, TTS, and video—into a unified ComfyUI canvas creates a single, exportable ecosystem.

More importantly, your decision to render characters on a green screen and composite them in Remotion is the **single most effective way to stabilize AI video**. Forcing a diffusion model to render a character, their motion, *and* a complex background simultaneously causes perspective warping and hallucinated geometry. By isolating the character on a solid green background and assembling the layers in code using Remotion's chroma key effects, you bypass the most expensive failure modes of generative video.

Here is how this architecture snaps together.

---

## 1. The Cloudflare Agent (The Orchestrator)

The Cloudflare Workers AI agent acts as your Assistant Director. Humans provide the high-level intent, and the agent translates that into the exact mathematical parameters the system needs.

* **Custom JSON Generation:** When a human inputs a scene premise (e.g., *"Elias interrogates the guard"*), the agent builds the JSON Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). It queries the database for character states and narrative canon, packaging them into the payload.
* **Dynamic Tone Parameter Tuning:** Instead of a human tweaking ComfyUI sliders, the agent dynamically adjusts them based on the scene's emotional context. If the database notes Elias is "exhausted and injured," the agent sets `curtness_slider: 0.9` and `pacing: 0.4` in the JSON payload before dispatching it to ComfyUI.
* **Text LoRA Routing:** The agent determines which character voices are needed and injects the specific local path or trigger tag for their fine-tuned text LoRAs (e.g., loading `elias_dialogue_v3.safetensors` into the LLM node) to ensure the generated text matches their exact idiom.

## 2. The Unified ComfyUI Graph (The Factory)

You build one massive, multi-modal pipeline inside ComfyUI using custom nodes. The canvas handles the entire generation sequence locally:

1. **The LLM Nodes:** Custom nodes (e.g., ComfyUI-Ollama or LLM Party integrations) receive the JSON payload from Cloudflare. They load the open-weights text model and the character-specific text LoRAs. The nodes output the actual written screenplay lines.
2. **The TTS Nodes:** The dialogue strings flow directly into audio generation nodes (like Parler-TTS or CosyVoice wrapped for ComfyUI), outputting `.wav` audio stems.
3. **The Math Nodes (Timeline Lock):** A simple math node calculates the audio duration, multiplies it by 24 fps, and passes the exact integer to the video sampler's `frame_count` input.
4. **The Greenscreen Video Nodes:** The visual diffusion pipeline receives the locked frame count. Its prompt is strictly constrained to generate the character on a flat, neon green `#00FF00` background. It ignores the environment entirely, focusing 100% of the GPU's VRAM on character silhouette and facial consistency.

## 3. Remotion (The Assembler & Compositor)

Remotion acts as both your animatic timeline and your final VFX compositor, utilizing standard web technologies to stack the layers.

### Phase A: The Radio Play

Before video is even rendered, Remotion pulls the TTS audio stems exported by ComfyUI. It sequences them programmatically on a timeline, layers in the Foley tracks, and outputs an audio-only MP4 (the animatic). This allows the human director to review the pacing and dialogue performance before authorizing the cloud GPU spend for the video pass.

### Phase B: The Compositing

Once the greenscreen video renders are complete, Remotion automatically handles the final assembly:

1. **Chroma Keying:** Using `@remotion/effects`, Remotion applies the `colorKey()` function to the ComfyUI video layer. This keys out the green background, leaving only the character with a transparent alpha channel.
2. **Environment Layering:** The transparent character layer is placed over a static, high-resolution background image (or a subtle 2D parallax setup).
3. **Camera & Polish:** Remotion code applies digital camera shakes, subtle zooms, and color grading across the entire composition, welding the AI character into the background.

---

## Visualizing the FlowIntegrating the script generation, TTS, and greenscreen video into a single ComfyUI graph—and offloading the compositing to Remotion—massively shifts the risk profile of this project.

Because you are now relying on software compositing (chroma keys) and chained multi-modal custom nodes (LLM $\rightarrow$ Audio $\rightarrow$ Math $\rightarrow$ Video), the build sequence must change. You must prove the visual fidelity and the local data flow before you ever rent a cloud server.

Here is the revised, step-by-step "Walking Skeleton" sequence to bring this specific architecture online safely.

---

### Step 1: The Compositing Proof (Local ComfyUI + Remotion)

Your highest visual risk is whether an AI-generated greenscreen character will composite cleanly over a background without horrific edge-fringing or floating-foot syndrome.

* **What to build:** Generate one single 3-second video of a character on a `#00FF00` background using ComfyUI on your local GPU. Write a basic Remotion composition that applies `@remotion/effects` `colorKey()` to remove the green and layers the character over a static background image.
* **What to test:** Does the chroma key hold up around hair and motion blur? Does the character look grounded?
* **Why first?** If the greenscreen aesthetic fails, the entire pipeline strategy collapses. Prove the final visual output before building the factory that makes it.

### Step 2: The Multi-Modal Graph (Local ComfyUI)

Your highest logic risk is routing text outputs directly into audio and video inputs within a visual node graph without human copy-pasting.

* **What to build:** Construct the unified "Factory" graph on your local workstation.
1. A Local LLM Node (loading a Text LoRA).
2. A TTS Audio Node (taking the LLM string).
3. A Math Node (Audio duration $\times$ 24 = frames).
4. The Greenscreen Video Sampler (taking the frame count).


* **What to test:** Hit "Queue Prompt." Ensure the LLM writes the line, the TTS speaks it, the math calculates the exact frames, and the video matches the length perfectly.
* **Why second?** You must lock the API-format JSON template. If the nodes cannot pass data to each other locally, they will fail in the cloud.

### Step 3: The Radio Play Engine (Remotion Phase 1)

Before spinning up expensive cloud GPUs, build the system that allows you to review the story.

* **What to build:** Extend your Remotion project to ingest the TTS audio stems exported by ComfyUI and sequence them on a timeline with basic text-on-screen indicating the action.
* **What to test:** Can you render a full 2-minute scene as an audio-only `.mp4` (the animatic) programmatically?

### Step 4: Scale-to-Zero Infrastructure (Cloudflare R2 + RunPod)

Now you transition from local prototyping to cloud execution.

* **What to build:** Set up your Cloudflare R2 bucket. Upload your models, LoRAs, and the locked ComfyUI API JSON from Step 2. Build the serverless bootstrap script on RunPod to download these assets via `s5cmd`, run the graph, and upload the final greenscreen video back to R2.
* **What to test:** Dispatch a raw JSON payload to the RunPod endpoint via Postman. Verify the worker boots, generates the video, uploads it, and shuts down.

### Step 5: The Production Coordinator (Cloudflare Workers + DO + D1)

With the GPU proven, wrap it in the safety harness.

* **What to build:** Deploy the Hono router and the `ShotCoordinator` Durable Object. Set up the Cloudflare D1 relational database to hold the Fact and Scene dependency tables.
* **What to test:** Send an inpaint or render request to the Worker. Verify the Durable Object enforces the idempotency key, dispatches to RunPod, catches the RunPod webhook, and successfully tracks the circuit breaker (`inpaint_attempt_index`).

### Step 6: The AI Agent & Dashboard (Workers AI + Astro)

Finally, build the brain that drives the car, and the steering wheel for the human.

* **What to build:** Connect Cloudflare Workers AI to generate the dynamic tone parameters (e.g., `curtness: 0.9`) and select the appropriate Text LoRAs. Build the Astro frontend where the human director inputs the high-level scene premise and views the final Remotion composites.
* **What to test:** Type "Elias interrogates the guard, heavily injured" into the Astro UI. Watch the Agent build the JSON, send it to the Durable Object, trigger the RunPod GPU, and display the final composited video on your screen.### Step 1: The Modular Subgraph Architecture & Data Contracts (Local)

Instead of building a monolithic canvas where text models, TTS engines, and diffusion pipelines compete for the same system RAM and VRAM, decouple the system into three isolated child graphs managed by a parent runner.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MASTER RUNNER / PARENT GRAPH                                           │
│                                                                        │
│  [Child Graph A: Dialogue] ──(AST JSON)──► [Child Graph B: Audio/Math] │
│                                                        │               │
│                                            (Frame Count Manifest)      │
│                                                        ▼               │
│                                            [Child Graph C: Video]      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

* **Child Graph A (`dialogue_generation.json`):** Contains the local LLM node with character-specific text LoRA loaders. Inputs: scene premise, tone parameters, character IDs. Output: serialized JSON containing speaker lines and emotional intent.
* **Child Graph B (`audio_timing.json`):** Contains the TTS engine (Parler-TTS, Chatterbox, or CosyVoice nodes) and foley placement. An internal math node measures the audio buffer length in milliseconds and runs:

$$\text{target\_frames} = \lceil (\text{duration\_ms} / 1000) \times 24 \rceil$$



Outputs: `.wav` audio stems and a clean JSON timing manifest (`{ shot_id, dialogue_file, target_frames }`).
* **Child Graph C (`greenscreen_video.json`):** The isolated diffusion graph. Takes `target_frames`, visual character LoRAs, and the locked `#00FF00` prompt to generate only the character visual plates.
* **What to prove:** Execute the parent-child handoff locally. A master script or parent node invokes Graph A, pipes its JSON to Graph B via API, catches the frame-count integer, and passes it into Graph C. VRAM must completely flush between Subgraph A/B execution and Subgraph C execution.

---

### Step 2: The Automated Radio Play Engine (Remotion Pre-Visualization)

Before any cloud video compute is provisioned, automate the audio verification layer to ensure that scene pacing, dialogue delivery, and shot durations work as a narrative unit.

* **What to build:** A Remotion project configured to watch the output directory of Child Graph B.
* **The Handoff:** Remotion reads the JSON timing manifest, programmatically places the dialogue `.wav` stems on individual audio tracks, inserts the foley beds, and renders a lightweight, audio-only animatic with simple lower-third text cards showing the dialogue and shot boundaries.
* **What to prove:** You can listen to the generated scene, evaluate the performance, and confirm that the audio timing feels right. If the pacing is off, you re-roll Child Graph A or adjust Child Graph B's parameters without having spent a single cent on video rendering.

---

### Step 3: Cloud Hydration & Headless Execution of Child Graph C (R2 + RunPod)

Because Child Graphs A and B run quickly on local compute, only Child Graph C (the heavy video diffusion model) needs to run on cloud serverless GPUs.

* **What to build:**
1. **Cloudflare R2 Bucket:** Store the Wan 2.2 / diffusion base checkpoints, character visual LoRAs, and the frozen `greenscreen_video.json` template.
2. **RunPod Serverless Container:** Create the headless worker image configured with `s5cmd` to pull weights from R2 into local NVMe on boot.


* **What to test:** Use a local terminal or Postman to send an HTTP POST to the RunPod endpoint with a hardcoded payload:
```json
{
  "shot_id": "ep01_sh04",
  "frame_count": 96,
  "prompt": "Elias shouting, neon green background (#00FF00), high contrast",
  "lora": "elias_visual_v2.safetensors"
}

```


Verify that the container boots, hydrates, renders the 96 frames of greenscreen footage, uploads the final MP4 to R2, and terminates.

---

### Step 4: The Edge Orchestrator & State Machine (Cloudflare Workers + Durable Objects + D1)

With the heavy GPU engine verified in isolation, bring online the state machine that coordinates execution and handles failure states.

* **What to build:**
1. **Cloudflare D1 Database:** Define the relational schema for the narrative dependency graph (Fact Table, Scene Table, and version-pinned edges).
2. **`ShotCoordinator` Durable Object:** Deploy the per-shot actor that manages the 2-retry circuit breaker, tracks idempotency keys, and serializes RunPod webhooks.
3. **Hono Webhook Ingestion:** An endpoint at `/api/webhooks/runpod` that validates incoming job completion signals and notifies the corresponding Durable Object.


* **What to test:** Send mock requests to `/api/shots/:shot_id/inpaint` with duplicate idempotency keys and verify they are rejected with HTTP 409. Trigger mock failures and ensure the circuit breaker trips cleanly after the second retry.

---

### Step 5: The Agentic Parameter Injector & Production Frontend (Cloudflare Agent + Astro)

Now that the execution engine and safety harnesses exist, build the control interface.

* **What to build:**
1. **Cloudflare Workers AI Agent:** A background agent that takes the high-level human premise, checks the D1 Fact table to verify narrative dependencies, selects the correct character text LoRA names, and writes the JSON payload for Child Graph A (including dynamic tone parameters like `curtness: 0.85` or `pacing: 0.4`).
2. **Astro Production Dashboard:** A web dashboard that allows the director to input the initial scene premise, view the Remotion Radio Play for approval, and trigger the cloud batch dispatch for Child Graph C.


* **What to test:** Input a premise in the Astro UI. Watch the Agent compile the JSON, run Child Graph A and B to generate the Radio Play, wait for human sign-off, and dispatch Child Graph C to RunPod—automatically producing the final composited scene in Remotion.Running text generation, audio synthesis, and high-parameter video diffusion within a single ComfyUI canvas will exceed the 24GB VRAM ceiling of consumer GPUs and create an unmaintainable web of execution links.

Decoupling the pipeline into three discrete, API-format child graphs managed by a local execution broker isolates memory footprints and enforces deterministic data contracts at each boundary.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        LOCAL EXECUTION BROKER                          │
│                                                                        │
│  1. Ingests Scene Premise & Tone Settings                              │
│  2. Dispatches Child Graph A (LLM + Text LoRA)                         │
│  3. Validates Dialogue AST Contract                                    │
│  4. Flushes VRAM via /free API                                         │
│  5. Dispatches Child Graph B (TTS + Audio Math)                        │
│  6. Validates Timing Manifest Contract                                 │
│  7. Dispatches Child Graph C (Greenscreen Video Diffusion)             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

---

### Step 1: Define the Data Contracts

Before configuring nodes, freeze the schemas that pass between subgraphs. Every child graph reads from or writes to these standardized JSON payloads.

**Contract 1: Dialogue AST (`Graph A -> Graph B`)**
Output by the LLM in Graph A; consumed by the TTS engine in Graph B:

```json
{
  "scene_id": "ep01_sc03",
  "shots": [
    {
      "shot_id": "sh_01",
      "character_id": "char_elias",
      "text_lora_trigger": "<lora:elias_dialogue_v3:0.85>",
      "dialogue_text": "The gate locks from the outside. We have under four minutes.",
      "emotion": "urgent_whisper",
      "foley_cues": ["distant_siren", "heavy_rain_loop"],
      "camera_intent": "medium_close_up"
    }
  ]
}

```

**Contract 2: Timing & Exposure Manifest (`Graph B -> Graph C / Remotion`)**
Output by the audio/math nodes in Graph B; consumed by the video sampler in Graph C and Remotion's animatic timeline:

```json
{
  "scene_id": "ep01_sc03",
  "shot_id": "sh_01",
  "character_id": "char_elias",
  "audio_stem_path": "outputs/audio/ep01_sc03_sh01_dialogue.wav",
  "duration_ms": 3850,
  "fps": 24,
  "target_frames": 93,
  "visual_prompt": "Elias speaking, tense jaw, neon green background (#00FF00), studio lighting",
  "visual_lora": "elias_actor_v4.safetensors"
}

```

---

### Step 2: Build Child Graph A (`dialogue_generation.json`)

Graph A handles semantic text extraction and character voice tuning on local compute.

* **Node 1: Local Model Loader (e.g., `OllamaLoader` / `LLM_Model_Loader`):** Mounts a quantized 14B/32B base model (such as Qwen 2.5 14B) into system RAM or partial offload.
* **Node 2: Text LoRA Applier:** Injects character-specific text adapters (e.g., fine-tuned weights capturing specific vocabulary, cadence, and colloquialisms).
* **Node 3: Parameter Ingestion Node:** Exposes input string/primitive slots for the scene premise, canon facts, and tone sliders (`curtness`, `aggression`, `evasiveness`).
* **Node 4: Schema Constrained Sampler:** Passes the system prompt with logit masking or guided decoding to guarantee the model outputs strictly valid JSON conforming to Contract 1.
* **Node 5: Save Text/JSON:** Writes the verified `dialogue_ast.json` to the project's local operational directory.

---

### Step 3: Build Child Graph B (`audio_timing.json`)

Graph B translates text strings into acoustic reality, generates foley beds, and determines shot length.

* **Node 1: JSON Load & Splitter:** Parses `dialogue_ast.json`, extracting `dialogue_text`, `character_id`, and `emotion` per `shot_id`.
* **Node 2: Character Voice Profile Selector:** Maps `character_id` to reference audio latents or voice embeddings (e.g., Parler-TTS voice descriptions or CosyVoice zero-shot speaker files).
* **Node 3: TTS Synthesizer:** Generates the speech waveform matching the emotional inflection.
* **Node 4: Audio Duration Probe (Custom Python Node):**
Reads the generated audio tensor length and applies the timing equation:

$$\text{target\_frames} = \left\lceil \frac{\text{duration\_ms}}{1000} \times 24 \right\rceil$$



Padding frames (e.g., +12 frames for pre/post dialogue breath room) are appended here.
* **Node 5: Audio Stem Export & Manifest Writer:** Saves `dialogue.wav` and outputs the compiled `timing_manifest.json` containing the exact frame target.

---

### Step 4: Build Child Graph C (`greenscreen_video.json`)

Graph C isolates the heavy diffusion pipeline, rendering character plates on a uniform chroma background.

* **Node 1: Manifest Parameter Receiver:** Exposes primitive integer and string slots for `target_frames`, `visual_prompt`, and `visual_lora`.
* **Node 2: Diffusion Model & LoRA Loader:** Loads the video model (e.g., Wan 2.2 / AnimateDiff) and binds the character appearance LoRA.
* **Node 3: Empty Latent Video Generator:** Accepts the `target_frames` integer from the manifest to allocate the exact latent dimensions:

$$\text{Latent Shape} = [B, C, \lceil \text{target\_frames} / 4 \rceil, H/8, W/8]$$


* **Node 4: Positive Conditioning Ingestion:** Injects the locked prompt string enforcing chroma keying:
```text
[visual_prompt], isolated on solid vivid green screen background, chroma key #00FF00, flat high-key studio lighting, crisp silhouettes, zero background clutter

```


* **Node 5: KSampler & VAE Decode:** Executes diffusion across the allocated frames and decodes to video frames.
* **Node 6: Video Output:** Exports `sh_01_greenscreen.mp4`.

---

### Step 5: Implement the Local Execution Broker

Instead of a monolithic UI canvas, a lightweight local script (Node.js or Python) orchestrates execution across ComfyUI’s REST API (`/prompt`, `/free`, `/history`). This enforces clean VRAM teardowns between modal stages.

```typescript
// scripts/run_local_modular_pipeline.ts
import fs from 'node:fs/promises';

const COMFY_API = 'http://127.0.0.1:8188';

async function queueWorkflow(workflowJson: Record<string, any>): Promise<string> {
  const res = await fetch(`${COMFY_API}/prompt`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ prompt: workflowJson })
  });
  const data = await res.json();
  return data.prompt_id;
}

async function flushVRAM(): Promise<void> {
  // Forces ComfyUI to purge loaded models and unmount weights from GPU memory
  await fetch(`${COMFY_API}/free`, {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ unload_models: true, free_memory: true })
  });
}

async function waitForCompletion(promptId: string): Promise<void> {
  let finished = false;
  while (!finished) {
    const res = await fetch(`${COMFY_API}/history/${promptId}`);
    const data = await res.json();
    if (data[promptId] && data[promptId].status?.completed) {
      finished = true;
    } else {
      await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 1000));
    }
  }
}

export async function runShotPipeline(shotConfig: { premise: string; tone: number }) {
  console.log('[1/4] Running Graph A: Script & Dialogue AST...');
  const graphA = JSON.parse(await fs.readFile('workflows/dialogue_generation.json', 'utf-8'));
  graphA['2'].inputs.premise = shotConfig.premise;
  graphA['2'].inputs.curtness = shotConfig.tone;
  const pidA = await queueWorkflow(graphA);
  await waitForCompletion(pidA);

  console.log('[2/4] Flushing VRAM...');
  await flushVRAM();

  console.log('[3/4] Running Graph B: TTS & Frame Calculation...');
  const graphB = JSON.parse(await fs.readFile('workflows/audio_timing.json', 'utf-8'));
  const pidB = await queueWorkflow(graphB);
  await waitForCompletion(pidB);

  console.log('[4/4] Reading Timing Manifest & Running Graph C: Greenscreen Video...');
  const manifest = JSON.parse(await fs.readFile('outputs/timing_manifest.json', 'utf-8'));
  
  const graphC = JSON.parse(await fs.readFile('workflows/greenscreen_video.json', 'utf-8'));
  graphC['3'].inputs.length = manifest.target_frames;
  graphC['6'].inputs.text = manifest.visual_prompt;
  const pidC = await queueWorkflow(graphC);
  await waitForCompletion(pidC);

  console.log(`[Success] Shot generated cleanly with exactly ${manifest.target_frames} frames.`);
}

```

This ensures the 14B text model unloads before TTS weights initialize, and all audio/text weights are completely flushed before the video diffusion model allocates its 16GB–22GB latent memory space on the GPU.To produce a rich, human-readable screenplay (with scene headers, action blocks, and parentheticals) while still feeding clean machine data into your downstream graphs, Child Graph A must follow a **Dual-Artifact Pattern**.

Rather than making two separate LLM calls, you instruct a local open-weights model (e.g., Qwen 2.5 14B or 32B via Ollama or llama.cpp) to return a structured JSON object containing two top-level keys:

1. `human_readable_script`: A standard Fountain/Markdown-formatted screenplay you can open and read in any text editor or screenwriting app.
2. `shots`: The machine-readable array of discrete dialogue stems, emotions, and camera prompts that Child Graph B and C need.

---

### 2. The ComfyUI Graph Architecture (`dialogue_generation.json`)

Inside ComfyUI, assemble Graph A using standard text/LLM custom nodes (e.g., `ComfyUI-Ollama` or `ComfyUI-LLM`):

```
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Primitive: Scene Setup  │
│ • Premise & Conflict    │
│ • Pacing & Tone Sliders │
└───────────┬─────────────┘
            │
            ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐
│ Ollama / Llama.cpp Node │◄─── Character Voice Prompt
│ • Model: Qwen 2.5 14B   │      (or Text LoRA injected via system prompt)
│ • Format: "json"        │
└───────────┬─────────────┘
            │ (Raw JSON String)
            ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Custom Node: "Script & AST Demuxer"                    │
│                                                        │
│ Output 1: String ──► Show Text / Save to `sc03.fountain`│
│ Output 2: JSON   ──► Save to `outputs/dialogue_ast.json`│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```

#### Node Breakdown:

* **Node 1: Scene Config (Primitive String & Float Nodes):**
* `premise`: *"Elias corners Vance on the docks. Vance is defiant; Elias is operating on pure exhaustion."*
* `curtness_slider`: `0.85` (0.0 = verbose/theatrical, 1.0 = monosyllabic/blunt).
* `threat_level`: `0.70`.


* **Node 2: Prompt Assembler (String Concatenate Node):**
Combines the character profile, the scene setup, and the structural instruction:
```text
You are writing a cinematic action screenplay scene.
Format your response as a valid JSON object matching the requested schema.
Include standard screenplay sluglines, vivid sensory action lines, and dialogue parentheticals in "human_readable_script".
Break down every speaking line into atomic entries in the "shots" array for downstream audio/video rendering.
Tone parameters: Curtness: {curtness}, Threat Level: {threat_level}.

```


* **Node 3: Ollama / Local LLM Generator:**
* Runs locally on your GPU (e.g., `qwen2.5:14b-instruct-q5_K_M`, requiring only ~10 GB VRAM).
* Enforces JSON output mode (`format: "json"`).


* **Node 4: The Custom Demuxer Node (Detailed below):**
Receives the raw JSON string from Node 3. It parses the object, writes the screenplay text to an `.md` or `.fountain` file for human reading, and writes the `shots` array to `outputs/dialogue_ast.json` for Child Graph B.

---

### 3. The Custom Python Node: `ScriptDemuxNode.py`

Place this lightweight script in your ComfyUI directory under `ComfyUI/custom_nodes/script_demuxer/script_demuxer.py`. It provides the bridge between human viewing and downstream automation.

```python
import json
import os

class ScriptDemuxNode:
    """
    Splits the dual-artifact LLM output into a human-readable script file
    and a validated machine-readable AST for Child Graph B.
    """
    @classmethod
    def INPUT_TYPES(cls):
        return {
            "required": {
                "raw_llm_json": ("STRING", {"multiline": True, "forceInput": True}),
                "scene_id": ("STRING", {"default": "ep01_sc01"}),
                "output_dir": ("STRING", {"default": "outputs"}),
            }
        }

    RETURN_TYPES = ("STRING", "STRING")
    RETURN_NAMES = ("human_script", "ast_json_path")
    FUNCTION = "demux_and_save"
    CATEGORY = "Pipeline/Scripting"

    def demux_and_save(self, raw_llm_json: str, scene_id: str, output_dir: str):
        try:
            data = json.loads(raw_llm_json)
        except Exception as e:
            raise ValueError(f"[ScriptDemuxNode] Invalid JSON emitted by LLM: {str(e)}")

        human_script = data.get("human_readable_script", "NO_SCRIPT_GENERATED")
        shots = data.get("shots", [])

        # Ensure destination directories exist
        script_dir = os.path.join(output_dir, "scripts")
        ast_dir = os.path.join(output_dir, "ast")
        os.makedirs(script_dir, exist_ok=True)
        os.makedirs(ast_dir, exist_ok=True)

        # 1. Save human-readable screenplay (.fountain / .md)
        script_path = os.path.join(script_dir, f"{scene_id}.fountain")
        with open(script_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            f.write(human_script)

        # 2. Save machine AST for Child Graph B
        ast_path = os.path.join(ast_dir, f"{scene_id}_ast.json")
        ast_payload = {
            "scene_id": scene_id,
            "shots": shots
        }
        with open(ast_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
            json.dump(ast_payload, f, indent=2)

        print(f"[ScriptDemuxNode] Wrote human screenplay to: {script_path}")
        print(f"[ScriptDemuxNode] Wrote pipeline AST to: {ast_path}")

        return (human_script, ast_path)

NODE_CLASS_MAPPINGS = {
    "ScriptDemuxNode": ScriptDemuxNode
}

NODE_DISPLAY_NAME_MAPPINGS = {
    "ScriptDemuxNode": "Script & AST Demuxer"
}

```

### 4. How to Play with This Locally Right Now

You don't need any cloud infrastructure, GPUs, or TTS models running to iterate on this step.

1. **Install Ollama locally:** Run `ollama run qwen2.5:14b`.
2. **Install ComfyUI-Ollama:** Clone `[https://github.com/stavrost/ComfyUI-Ollama](https://github.com/stavrost/ComfyUI-Ollama)` into your `ComfyUI/custom_nodes/` folder.
3. **Add `ScriptDemuxNode.py`:** Drop the script above into `ComfyUI/custom_nodes/script_demuxer/`.
4. **Boot ComfyUI:** Wire the **Ollama Generate** node into the **Script & AST Demuxer** node. Connect a **Show Text** node to `human_script`.
5. **Run the prompt:** Hit "Queue Prompt."

The ComfyUI canvas displays the fully formatted, cinematic screenplay right inside the UI, while silently dropping `ep01_sc03_ast.json` onto your hard drive—ready to trigger audio stems and frame calculations the moment you build Graph B.### System Prompt

```text
You are an expert cinematic screenwriter and technical narrative director. 
Your task is to generate a scene that fulfills two simultaneous requirements in a single, valid JSON object:
1. "human_readable_script": A fully realized screenplay formatted in clean Fountain/Markdown syntax (sluglines, character cues, parentheticals, evocative action descriptions).
2. "shots": A machine-readable array of discrete audiovisual shot objects designed for automated TTS, Foley synthesis, and video diffusion.

CRITICAL RULES:
- OUTPUT FORMAT: Output strictly valid JSON. Do not include markdown code fences (```json ... ```) outside the root object.
- DIALOGUE PARITY: The dialogue in "human_readable_script" and the "dialogue_text" in "shots" MUST match verbatim. Every spoken line in the screenplay must map to exactly one shot in the array in chronological order.
- ESCAPING: Use "\n" for all line breaks within the "human_readable_script" string. Never output unescaped literal newlines inside JSON string values.
- PARAMETER MAPPINGS:
  * curtness (0.0 to 1.0): At >= 0.7, characters speak in fragments, ellipses, and sentences under 8 words. At <= 0.3, characters use full clauses and layered explanations.
  * threat_level (0.0 to 1.0): At >= 0.7, subtext drops; physical leverage, weapons, and irreversible stakes dominate dialogue and parentheticals.
  * pacing (0.0 to 1.0): At >= 0.7, action lines are telegraphic (1-2 sentences max per block), emphasizing rapid physical beats over reflection.

```

### Key Settings for 14B Local Inference (Ollama / Llama.cpp)

* **Temperature:** `0.55` – `0.65`. Higher values cause 14B models to drop JSON punctuation or invent extraneous shot properties; lower values make dialogue sound repetitive.
* **Top-P:** `0.90`.
* **Repeat Penalty:** `1.12`. Essential for preventing looping action lines during high-pacing configurations.
* **Context Window (`num_ctx`):** Set to at least **8192**. The system prompt and few-shot block consume ~1,800 tokens; generating the dual output needs 2,000–3,000 tokens of generation buffer.
* **Structured Output Enforcement:** In Ollama, use the `format: "json"` flag. If running via llama.cpp or vLLM, compile a GBNF grammar using the JSON schema to make syntax errors mathematically impossible at the logit level.The Automated Radio Play Engine uses Remotion to programmatically compile your JSON timing manifest and TTS audio stems into a lightweight, reviewable animatic. This completely bypasses the need for manual timeline editing software, allowing you to review pacing before spending money on cloud GPUs.

## Ingestion and Dynamic Metadata

Remotion requires a predefined composition duration before rendering. Because your scene length varies based on the AI-generated TTS output, you must use Remotion's `calculateMetadata` API to establish the timeline dynamically.

* Parse the `timing_manifest.json` generated by Child Graph B upon initialization.
* Iterate through the `shots` array, fetching the exact duration of each local `.wav` file using `@remotion/media-utils` and the `getAudioDurationInSeconds` function.
* Multiply each duration by your global `fps` (24) and apply `Math.ceil()` to determine the exact integer frame boundaries.
* Return the summed `durationInFrames` to the root `<Composition>`, locking the master timeline length automatically.

## The React Composition Tree

With the metadata calculated, the engine maps the JSON shots array into a sequence of isolated, time-bound React components.

* Wrap each shot in a `<Sequence>` component, passing the calculated start frame (`from`) and length (`durationInFrames`).
* Mount the `<Audio ...")}" src="{staticFile("/>` component inside the sequence to guarantee perfect dialogue synchronization.
* Render an `<AbsoluteFill>` containing basic HTML typography to display the `shot_id`, `dialogue_text`, and `camera_intent` directly on the screen.

## Foley and Multi-Track Layering

A dry TTS voice is difficult to evaluate for cinematic pacing. The engine natively stacks concurrent audio layers using React's component hierarchy.

* Map the `foley_cues` array from the manifest to pre-existing ambient tracks (e.g., `heavy_rain.wav`).
* Mount these ambient tracks in a parallel React tree, spanning the entire composition length independently of the dialogue clips.
* Apply volume interpolation (`interpolate`) bound to the current frame to dynamically duck ambient sound during active dialogue.

## Headless Rendering Pipeline

This system runs entirely via the command line as a Node.js process, requiring zero graphical interface interaction or browser rendering.

* Configure a Node script utilizing `@remotion/bundler` to package the React code locally.
* Pass the bundled application URL to the `@remotion/renderer` using the `renderMedia()` function.
* Output a heavily compressed `H264` MP4 in seconds, ready for the director's approval before cloud GPU dispatch.The Automated Radio Play Engine transforms asynchronous TTS audio stems and JSON narrative ASTs into a frame-accurate, time-locked audiovisual animatic. It acts as the single source of temporal truth for the entire pipeline, establishing the hard duration constraints required before dispatching headless video diffusion models.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                       AUTOMATED RADIO PLAY PIPELINE                          │
│                                                                              │
│  [ timing_manifest.json ] ──► [ calculateMetadata() ]                        │
│                                      │                                       │
│                                      ▼ (Resolve Frame Boundaries & Padding)  │
│                                                                              │
│  [ React Composition Tree ] ◄────────┴────────┐                              │
│         │                                     │                              │
│         ├─► Track 1: Isolated Dialogue Stems  │                              │
│         ├─► Track 2: Spot Foley Cues          ├─► Audio Ducking Math         │
│         ├─► Track 3: Ambient Sound Bed        │                              │
│         └─► Visual: Production Slate & HUD    │                              │
│                                               │                              │
│  [ Headless Rendering CLI ] ◄─────────────────┘                              │
│         │                                                                    │
│         ▼                                                                    │
│  [ scene_animatic.mp4 ] ──► Director Review ──► Pinned Video Dispatch        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

```
